name: Yiddish

ancestors.notes: Core Germanic vocabulary from Middle High German; also Slavic and Hebrew/Aramaic components

notes: Eastern Yiddish in YIVO orthography — pointed, with the historical unpointed spelling of the Hebrew-Aramaic component retained (⟨ח⟩ ⟨ת⟩ ⟨שׂ⟩ ⟨כּ⟩ ⟨תּ⟩) and the five final forms ⟨ך ם ן ף ץ⟩ in use; neither holds in Soviet orthography, which respells the Hebrew-Aramaic component phonetically. Unlike Hebrew, Yiddish writes its vowels with letters. Written right-to-left. The pointing is part of the spelling, not an optional aid: ⟨אַ⟩ /a/ and ⟨אָ⟩ /ɔ/ are distinct letters, dagesh distinguishes ⟨פּ⟩ /p/ from ⟨פ⟩ /f/ and rafe ⟨בֿ⟩ /v/ from ⟨ב⟩ /b/, and the sin dot ⟨שׂ⟩ /s/ from bare ⟨ש⟩ /ʃ/. Shtumer alef ⟨א⟩ before ⟨י⟩ or ⟨ו⟩ is silent and marks that the syllable opens with the vocalic reading of that letter. The vowels of the unpointed Hebrew-Aramaic component are not recoverable from the letters and are a ceiling on any letter-driven transcription of Yiddish, not a gap in this description. Khirik yud ⟨יִ⟩ is a separate letter whose job after another yud is to block the tsvey-yudn reading, so ⟨ייִ⟩ is /ji/ and is keyed to defeat the longer-but-wrong maximal-munch match on ⟨יי⟩ /ɛɪ/ — ⟨ייִד⟩ is [jid], not [ɛɪd]. Maqaf ⟨־⟩, geresh ⟨׳⟩ and gershayim ⟨״⟩ are punctuation, not letters, and are deliberately not keyed.

location.notes: Glottolog's representative point for Eastern Yiddish.

allophone_rules.notes: Nasal place assimilation: /n/ is dorsal before a dorsal stop (⟨אָנקומען⟩, ⟨זינגען⟩). The following stop is retained, so ⟨נג⟩ is [ŋɡ], not [ŋ].

Yiddish phonology (Wikipedia): '[m] and [ŋ] appear as syllable nuclei as well, but only as allophones of /n/, after bilabial consonants and dorsal consonants, respectively.' This is the bilabial half — ⟨לעבן⟩ [ˈlɛbm̩].
The dorsal half of the same statement in YI_N_SYLL_BILABIAL — ⟨יאָגן⟩ [ˈjɔɡŋ̩].

Yiddish phonology (Wikipedia): the sonorants /l/ and /n/ function as syllable nuclei, e.g. אָװנט /ˈɔvn̩t/. Word-final ⟨ן⟩ with no vowel letter before it spells that nucleus (⟨שרײַבן⟩, ⟨העלפֿן⟩); after a vowel letter the ⟨ע⟩ carries the nucleus and ⟨ן⟩ stays a plain coda.
The /l/ half of the same syllabic-sonorant statement — אײזל /ˈɛɪzl̩/.

stress.notes: Jewish Language Project, Yiddish (Eastern): 'Stress in Germanic words usually falls on the first syllable of the word's root.' The same page states that unstressed vowels are typically reduced, which is what the ⟨ע⟩ nucleus_unstressed entry describes. Slavic and Semitic loanwords take penultimate stress and are not covered by this default; neither are separable prefixes, which are unstressed before the stem.
